strengths: Well-motivated problem with compelling Pass@N analysis showing better policies exist
Principled KL-regularized MDP formulation with rigorous theoretical analysis
Novel Theorem 2 (Reference-KL Tightening) proving learned policies generate distributions closer to data than reference
Memory-efficient training design leveraging frozen MDM features (only 134M added parameters)
Comprehensive evaluation across 4 diverse benchmarks with consistent improvements
Thorough experimental ablations demonstrating regularization effectiveness and method robustness
Generally clear presentation with detailed proofs and reproducible algorithms
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: primarily applies existing GRPO framework; Theorem 1 is restatement from Mroueh 2025
Modest empirical improvements on practical tasks (1-2% on language modeling; strongest 11.2% gains on puzzles)
Unrealistic theoretical assumptions (ideal MDM with zero loss, support containment) creating gap between theory and practice
Task-specific reference policy selection required (max-conf vs Top-K) with no principled procedure, limiting applicability and suggesting per-task tuning is needed
Evaluation limited to single architecture (LLaDA-8B); generalization unclear
Missing direct empirical comparison with concurrent DCOLT despite claimed differences
Theoretical-practical gap in surrogate losses (Propositions 1-3 rely on approximations; max-conf version uses CE instead of KL)
No error bars/confidence intervals in main results; statistical significance unclear
Hyperparameter choices (β, K, reward binning) lack thorough justification and ablation
Limited analysis of what learned policies learn differently from heuristics or when/why method fails

strengths: Clear problem motivation with convincing Pass@N analysis demonstrating superior unmasking orderings exist
Principled KL-regularized MDP formulation with convergence guarantees (Theorem 1) and new KL-tightening result (Theorem 2)
Comprehensive experiments across 4 benchmarks with strong gains on structured tasks (SUDOKU: 11.2% over max-confidence)
Memory-efficient implementation (134M policy on 8B MDM with frozen base model)
Thorough ablations studying regularization power and multiple reference policy realizations
Rigorous theoretical proofs for surrogate losses (Propositions 1-3) enabling practical optimization
Qualitative analysis with clear visualization of learned vs. heuristic unmasking trajectories
weaknesses: Limited core methodological novelty: primarily applies existing GRPO framework (Mroueh 2025) to unmasking; Theorem 2 largely follows from prior work
Improvements are highly task-dependent and collapse on realistic benchmarks (11.2% SUDOKU → 2% GSM8K → 0% MATH500), raising serious generalization concerns
Dense reward design with auxiliary log-probability signal for GSM8K/MATH500 obscures whether gains come from learned policy or reward engineering; no ablation on auxiliary signal contribution
Weak comparison with concurrent work DCOLT (Huang et al. 2025): only indirect comparison via ablation in Figure 3, not direct benchmarking on all tasks
No cross-dataset generalization: trained policies not evaluated on different benchmarks; Appendix D.2 preference-reward experiments are preliminary
Theorem 2 requires strong assumptions (ideal MDM with LMDM(θ*)=0, well-defined rewards, support containment) that don't hold in practice; gap between theory and practice unclear
Hyperparameter sensitivity not thoroughly studied: β=10^-4 critical but minimally ablated; different realizations optimal for different tasks suggests brittleness
No statistical rigor: Table 2 lacks confidence intervals or standard deviations; critical for borderline improvements, especially MATH500 tie with baseline
Comparison with DCOLT limited and generalization questions unaddressed despite DCOLT's similar approach to the same problem
